neighbours.label: ' with' opening a fronted manner or circumstance phrase in formal or literary prose ('It is with regret that', '. With a sigh, she'), vs ' with' as an ordinary complement
fire: Dear Sir, it is with sincere sorrow that I report the death of your uncle.
The door creaked open. With a heavy sigh, the widow stepped inside.
Ladies and gentlemen, it is with pride that I present this year's award.
The storm broke at midnight. With great effort the sailors lowered the sails.
Madam, it is with regret that we must decline your kind invitation.
He read the letter twice. With trembling fingers he folded it away.
The council met in haste. With regard to the bridge, nothing was decided.
The hounds drew near. With a desperate cry the stag leapt into the river.
quiet: Dear Sir, I report with sincere sorrow the death of your uncle.
The door creaked open, and the widow stepped inside quietly.
Ladies and gentlemen, I am proud to present this year's award.
The storm broke at midnight, and the sailors lowered the sails.
Madam, we must regretfully decline your kind invitation.
He read the letter twice and folded it away.
The council met in haste about the bridge, but nothing was decided.
The hounds drew near, and the stag leapt into the river.

Probe: 'It is with great pleasure' 0.260; every ordinary ' with' (mix with, room with a smile) 0.001-0.002; sentence-initial 'With trembling hands' scored 0.002 because it was the first token, so fire items put the fronted With after an earlier sentence.
